headline: Rocket Lab: record $268 million revenue and backlog up 52% to $3.6 billion on $1 billion of new launch deals; shares jump 18%
takeaway: Revenue rose 73% to a record $268 million and backlog jumped 52% in a single quarter to $3.57 billion, including $515 million of contracts for the still-unlaunched Neutron rocket at higher prices. The net loss widened to $0.12 a share, but operating cash flow turned positive and the shares rose 18%.
results: Rocket Lab reported revenue of $268 million for the third quarter, up 73% from $155 million and $34 million above the second quarter. The net loss widened to $79.7 million, or $0.12 a share, from $18.3 million a year earlier, when a tax benefit flattered the result; the loss before tax was $76.2 million against $59.3 million. GAAP operating cash flow was positive at $7.2 million.

Backlog reached a record $3.57 billion, up 52% since June. The company signed about $1 billion of launch contracts across Electron, the hypersonic test vehicle HASTE and Neutron, taking its launch backlog to 117 missions, plus $470 million of space-systems work. Neutron contracts worth more than $515 million from constellation operators took its pre-launch backlog to 16 missions, with the base price for several raised to $70 million.

Twelve Rocket Lab-built spacecraft reached orbit, including eight platforms for Globalstar’s direct-to-device constellation, two NASA Mars science spacecraft and the VICTUS HAZE responsive-space mission for the US Space Force. More than 55 spacecraft are in production.
mgmt: Founder and chief executive Sir Peter Beck called it a defining quarter, saying the end-to-end strategy is working as designed, with critical missions increasingly relying on Rocket Lab for launch, spacecraft and components, sometimes on a single mission. Neutron’s first launch is now targeted for no earlier than 2027, with first flight hardware delivered to Launch Complex 3.

For the fourth quarter Rocket Lab expects revenue of $270 to $290 million, GAAP gross margin of 34% to 36% and an adjusted EBITDA loss of $14 to $20 million. It has fully funded its pending acquisition of satellite operator Iridium Communications through an at-the-market share offering, secured lender approval to keep Iridium’s credit facility and won Iridium shareholders’ approval.
view: Rocket Lab has become the clear number two in Western launch behind SpaceX and, increasingly, a satellite manufacturer that can build, launch and operate a mission end to end. This quarter’s backlog jump is the most important number in the release. Signing $1.5 billion of new work in three months — and raising Neutron’s price to $70 million before it has flown — tells you that launch capacity is scarce and that constellation operators want an alternative to SpaceX badly enough to pay for it.

The Iridium deal changes the company’s character. Iridium brings a profitable, cash-generating satellite network with a long-standing US government customer base, which would give Rocket Lab recurring service revenue to offset the lumpy, loss-making launch and manufacturing businesses. It also brings Iridium’s debt and a much larger share count, funded by an equity offering that has diluted existing shareholders. Investors are betting the combination becomes a vertically integrated space company in the mould of SpaceX’s Starlink model, on a smaller scale.

The risks are timing and valuation. Neutron has slipped repeatedly and now will not fly before 2027; its 16-mission backlog depends on the first flights succeeding, and a failure would be costly both financially and reputationally. Rocket Lab is still loss-making, and at close to $30 billion of market value it trades at roughly 29 times this year’s expected revenue. The backlog provides visibility, but the share price assumes Neutron, the Iridium integration and the spacecraft business all deliver.
watch: Watch Neutron’s first-launch date and test milestones, the closing and integration of Iridium, conversion of the $3.6 billion backlog into revenue, and progress toward positive adjusted EBITDA.
